Entender o que são casos, ver o mapa dos: Understand what cases are, see the map of the six cases, and recognise which case appears, and why, in sentences you already know.
(ou: o caso da ação — e a pergunta que r: (or: the case of the action — and the one question that settles everything: is it animate?)
Uma cena que você já viveu (ou vai viver: A scene you have lived (or will). Picture it. You are in Russia. You have studied the alphabet, nouns, adjectives, verbs in the present, past and future. You feel confident. You walk into a shop, point at something and say: — Я ви́жу кни́га. The shop assistant understands, but winces. She repeats it, correcting you: — Я ви́жу кни́гу. You look again. It is the same word, кни́га, but now it ends in -у, not -а. You think: "Why? I learned that кни́га is feminine. Why did the ending change?" This happens to every Russian learner, and it happens because you have just met the accusative case. It sounds complicated, but it is not. Five minutes of careful reading will save you years of false immersion. What English already does. English has almost no cases, but it keeps a trace of this one in its pronouns. You say "I see him", never "I see he". You say "She loves me", never "She loves I". "Him", "her", "me", "us", "them", "whom" are the accusative (the object form) of he, she, I, we, they, who. Russian does the same with pronouns (я → меня, он → его), and, unlike English, it does it with nouns too. The case of action. The accusative is the case of the thing the action is done to. When you say "I read the book", "the book" is the object of the action. In English you know it is the object only because of word order (it comes after the verb). Russian lets the ending carry that job, which is why the word order can be freer. This object needs a special mark in Russian. That mark is the accusative case.
Animado e inanimado: quem «tem alma»: Animate and inanimate: who "has a soul"
A cosmovisão russa: quem tem alma?. Agor: The Russian view: who has a soul? Now comes the most fascinating part. Pay attention, because here is the key to everything. In Russian grammar, only people and animals "have a soul" (this is the traditional teaching image; grammarians call it animate versus inanimate). People have a soul. Animals have a soul. Objects don't. Plants don't. Ideas don't. A house has no soul. A stone has no soul. But a friend does. A dog does. A child does. What does this have to do with grammar? Everything. Because only those with a soul get special treatment in the accusative. Only they change form when they are the object of the action. I'll explain with the magic question: does the word have a soul? If YES → it is "animate" and gets a special mark in the accusative (in the masculine). If NO → it is "inanimate" and does not change in the accusative (in the masculine). Examples: Does Дом (house) have a soul? No. A house is an object, so it does not change in the accusative. Стол (table)? No, so it does not change. Друг (friend)? Yes, a person, so it changes in the accusative. Студент (student)? Yes, a person, so it changes. Собака (dog)? Yes, an animal. But wait: «собака» is feminine, and for the feminine the rule is different. We will get there. Keep this question in your head. It will solve 90% of your accusative mistakes. The single rule that solves it all. Before the details, here is the rule in one sentence. Memorise it: FEMININE: ALWAYS CHANGES. It makes no difference whether it has a soul or not. Always. MASCULINE: DEPENDS ON THE SOUL. If it has a soul, it changes. If not, it does not change. NEUTER: NEVER CHANGES. It is neuter, by nature. That is all. Three lines. You have just learned the accusative of nouns. Now the details.
O FEMININO — sempre muda. O feminino é o: The FEMININE: it always changes. The feminine is the easiest because it is consistent. It always changes, whether it has a soul or not. Feminine ending in -А → becomes -У. You drop the -а and put -у. As simple as that. Feminine ending in -Я → becomes -Ю. You drop the -я and put -ю. As simple as that. Feminine ending in -Ь → DOES NOT CHANGE. The feminine in -ь stays the same as the nominative. Attention: how do you know whether a feminine word will change? Look at the ending. Ends in -а → changes to -у. Ends in -я → changes to -ю. Ends in -ь → no change. And the soul? For the feminine it does not matter. The rule is always the same, with a soul or without. That is why the feminine is the easiest.
Caso: a função da palavra na frase: Case: the function of a word in the sentence
Em português, a função de uma palavra ap: In English, the function of a word shows in word order and prepositions: «the dog bit the man» is not «the man bit the dog». In Russian, the function shows in the ending: the word changes its ending, and each ending is a case. There are six cases. In «Мама читает книгу», «мама» is who does the action (nominative) and «книгу» is what receives the action (accusative). You have already used four of the six cases without knowing their names; now they get names.
o português não muda os substantivos, ma: English does not change its nouns, but it does change its pronouns: «I / me», «he / him». Russian does this with every word.

O MASCULINO — depende da alma: The MASCULINE: it depends on the soul
O MASCULINO — depende da alma. Agora, o: The MASCULINE: it depends on the soul. Now the masculine. Here the magic question comes in: does it have a soul? Masculine INANIMATE (no soul) → DOES NOT CHANGE. If the word is masculine and has no soul (an object, an idea, a place, a thing), it does not change in the accusative. It stays the same as the nominative. Notice: the word is identical. Дом is дом in the nominative and in the accusative. Example sentences follow. All inanimate objects stay the same: no mark, no change. Masculine ANIMATE (with a soul) → CHANGES (add one letter). If the word is masculine and has a soul (a person or an animal), it changes in the accusative. The change: add -А at the end (or -Я, if the word ends in -ь or -й). Rule: a masculine animate word ending in a consonant → +А. A masculine animate word ending in -ь → becomes -Я. A masculine animate word ending in -й → becomes -Я. Notice that you don't cut any letter. You add one at the end, -А or -Я. Example sentences follow. Notice that every word with a soul changed, and every one added a letter. The magic question in practice. Here is how to use the magic question to decide whether a masculine word changes. That is all. Ask. Answer. Apply. (Note that the animate masculine accusative is the same as the genitive: you will meet that in the next lessons.)
We are waiting for the doctor.
An object: it does not change.
A place: it does not change.
Neutro, tabela mestra e regra do acusati: The neuter, the master table and the accusative rule
PASSO 1: O NEUTRO — nunca muda. O neutro: STEP 1: The NEUTER: it never changes. The neuter is the easiest of all. It never changes in the accusative. It makes no difference whether it is an object, an idea or a thing. It stays the same as the nominative. Always. Notice that no neuter word changes. Ever. Example sentences follow. That is it. The neuter is neuter: no soul, no masculine/feminine endings to swap, no change. Full stop. STEP 2: The master table of the accusative. Here is the table that solves everything. STEP 3: The rule in three lines. If you forget everything else, memorise this: FEMININE: ALWAYS CHANGES (а→у, я→ю, ь does not change). MASCULINE: ASK "HAS IT GOT A SOUL?". If yes, add -а/-я. If not, no change. NEUTER: NEVER CHANGES. That is it. You have just mastered the accusative of nouns.

Genitivo: como formar e quando usar: Genitive: how to form it and when to use it
O genitivo responde a «кого? чего?». Voc: The genitive answers «кого? чего?». You use it (1) to say something does not exist: «У меня нет сестры»; (2) to say the owner: «книга брата»; (3) to say the origin: «из Бразилии»; (4) after certain prepositions: у, из, от, для, без, около, после; (5) with quantities: «чашка кофе». Formation in the singular: -а becomes -ы; -я becomes -и; a final consonant gains -а; masculine -й and -ь become -я; -о becomes -а; -е becomes -я; feminine -ь becomes -и. After г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, щ you write -и, never -ы.
Diga: «Кофе без сахара. Подарок для мамы: Say: «Кофе без сахара. Подарок для мамы. Книга брата. Нет сестры.»

Casos especiais (мать, дочь) e tabelas d: Special cases (мать, дочь) and support tables for the accusative
Casos especiais. МАТЬ e ДОЧЬ Duas palavr: Special cases. МАТЬ and ДОЧЬ. Two feminine words in -ь. In the singular they behave like any other feminine in -ь: they do not change. Мать is мать, дочь is дочь. In the plural they are irregular: the accusative plural is матере́й and дочере́й (the same as the genitive plural). You only need to remember this when you reach the plural. ДИТЯ. Дитя́ (child) is the only neuter word that names a person. In the accusative singular it stays дитя́ (the same as the nominative). In the plural it is дете́й (the same as the genitive plural). It is an exception, but you already know that дитя is special. СУДЬЯ. Судья́ (judge) is masculine in meaning but feminine in form (it ends in -я). In the accusative it changes like a feminine noun: судью́. Support tables: personal pronouns, adjectives and possessives in the accusative. English comparison: this is the part English still has. Just as "he" becomes "him" and "she" becomes "her", Russian я becomes меня́ and она́ becomes её.

Erros comuns no acusativo, frases e quad: Common accusative mistakes, sentences and summary chart
PASSO 1: Os erros que o brasileiro VAI c: STEP 1: The mistakes English speakers WILL make in the accusative. Mistake 1: using the nominative instead of the accusative for a feminine noun. ❌ Wrong: Я ви́жу кни́га. ✅ Right: Я ви́жу кни́гу. English nouns never change after the verb, so you think "book is book". But a feminine noun always changes in Russian. Always. Mistake 2: not changing an animate masculine. ❌ Wrong: Я ви́жу друг. ✅ Right: Я ви́жу дру́га. A "friend" has a soul. It changes. Always. Mistake 3: changing an inanimate masculine. ❌ Wrong: Я ви́жу до́ма. ✅ Right: Я ви́жу дом. A "house" has no soul. It does not change. Never. Mistake 4: forgetting that the neuter never changes. ❌ Wrong: Я ви́жу окна́. ✅ Right: Я ви́жу окно́. The neuter never changes. Never. Mistake 5: thinking that the feminine in -ь changes. ❌ Wrong: Я ви́жу дверю́. ✅ Right: Я ви́жу дверь. The feminine in -ь stays the same as the nominative. Mistake 6: applying the animate-masculine rule to a feminine word that names an animal. ❌ Wrong: Я ви́жу соба́к. The dog has a soul, so you might want to add a letter like for a masculine. But соба́ка is feminine, and a feminine always follows the feminine rule: а → у. ✅ Right: Я ви́жу соба́ку. The soul only matters for masculine nouns. Mistake 7: not telling an animate masculine from an inanimate one. This is the most serious error. Both стол and друг end in a consonant, and you cannot see the difference by looking. The magic question solves it: does стол have a soul? No. Does друг have a soul? Yes. STEP 2: Full sentences with the accusative. Now real sentences, to see the accusative at work. Dativo e instrumental: só o essencial: Dative and instrumental: just the essentials
O dativo responde a «кому?» (para quem,: The dative answers «кому?» (to whom, for whom): masculine -у or -ю (брат → брату), feminine -е (мама → маме). The pronouns change a lot: я → мне, ты → тебе, он → ему, она → ей, мы → нам, вы → вам, они → им. One important sentence: «Мне нравится музыка» (literally «to me is pleasing the music» = I like music). The instrumental answers «кем?» and is the form for «with someone» (with = «с»): masculine -ом or -ем (брат → с братом), feminine -ой or -ей (мама → с мамой). This is only a first contact: each case will get its own lessons.
I give the book to my brother.
Eu tenho um amigo. Ele se chama Ivan. Eu: I have a friend. His name is Ivan. I often call him. We like to walk together. Ivan works with his brother. I like Ivan.
Say: «Я звоню маме. Я работаю с другом. Мне нравится музыка.»
